candidates.section: Management's Discussion and Analysis — Credit risk — Credit risk limits
candidates.company_disclosed_text: Concentration risk is defined as the risk arising from an overexposure in particular industry sectors, countries, or credit products within the portfolio, reflecting the potential for credit deterioration and default to be relatively highly correlated.
candidates.our_interpretation: Framework, not oil-specific: RBC treats industry-sector overexposure as a correlated-default risk. It is the lens for reading the oil-and-gas rows in Tables 41 and 72-74.
anchors: Credit concentration limits are reviewed on a regular basis after considering business, economic, financial and regulatory environments.
candidates.context_before: …levels: single name; regional, country and industrial sector (notional and economic capital); regulatory large exposure; product and portfolio; and underwriting and distribution. These limits apply across all businesses, portfolios, transactions and products. We actively manage credit exposures and limits to ensure alignment with our risk appetite, to maintain our target business mix and to ensure that there is no undue concentration risk.
candidates.context_after: Credit concentration limits are reviewed on a regular basis after considering business, economic, financial and regulatory environments. candidates.section: Management's Discussion and Analysis — Credit risk exposure by portfolio, sector and geography (Table 41)
candidates.our_interpretation: Disclosed fact: oil-and-gas EAD of $18,880 million at October 31, 2025 (2024: $19,107 million). Our arithmetic, not RBC's: about 0.83% of total EAD ($2,272,558 million) and 1.34% of total wholesale EAD. Almost half (8,671) is undrawn commitments, which could be drawn under stress.

candidates.section: Note 2 Summary of material accounting policies, estimates and judgments — Allowance for credit losses — Use of forward-looking information
candidates.company_disclosed_text: Macroeconomic variables used in our expected credit loss models include, but are not limited to, unemployment rates, gross domestic product growth rates, equity return indices, commodity prices and Canadian housing prices.
candidates.our_interpretation: Mechanism: commodity prices are an input to RBC's expected-credit-loss models, so an oil price shock can change allowances through forward-looking scenarios. RBC does not say how large that effect is or which commodities are used.
anchors: Note 2 Summary of material accounting policies, estimates and judgments
candidates.context_before: …to estimate Stage 1 and Stage 2 credit loss allowances are modelled based on the macroeconomic variables (or changes in macroeconomic variables) that are most closely correlated with credit losses in the relevant portfolio. Each macroeconomic scenario used in our expected credit loss calculation includes a projection of all relevant macroeconomic variables used in our models for a five-year period, subsequently reverting to long-run averages.
candidates.context_after: Depending on their usage in the models, macroeconomic variables may be projected at a country, province/state or more granular level. Our estimation of expected credit losses in Stage 1 and Stage 2 is a discounted probability-weighted estimate that considers a minimum of three future macroeconomic scenarios. candidates.section: Note 5 Loans and allowance for credit losses — Key inputs and assumptions — Scenario design and weightings
candidates.company_disclosed_text: During Q2 2025, in response to U.S. international trade policy, we designed a trade disruption scenario to replace our energy sector scenario.
candidates.our_interpretation: Disclosed fact: RBC had an energy-sector downside scenario and replaced it in Q2 2025. Our reading: management judged trade disruption a more relevant downside than an energy shock for fiscal 2025 allowances. This is not evidence that energy risk disappeared.
candidates.context_before: …2026 and for the U.S. unemployment rate to rise, peaking in calendar Q1 2026, followed by a return to equilibrium by calendar Q4 2026. The central bank policy rate in Canada is expected to remain unchanged until the end of calendar 2026 and cuts are expected in the U.S. until the middle of calendar 2026. Our downside scenarios include two additional and more severe downside scenarios designed for trade disruptions and the real estate sector.
candidates.context_after: Our downside scenarios reflect the possibility of moderate and escalating macroeconomic shocks beginning in calendar Q1 2026 relative to our base scenario. In these scenarios, conditions are expected to deteriorate from calendar Q4 2025 levels for up to 18 months, followed by a recovery for the remainder of the period. hypotheses_not_documented.hypothesis: Oil-price declines raise RBC's credit losses through oil-and-gas borrowers.
hypotheses_not_documented.status: Not supported by FY2025 data: oil-and-gas PCL was $6M (2024: -$51M) and EAD is about 0.8% of total. Indirect channels (Alberta consumer and commercial credit, ECL scenarios) are undisclosed by sector.
hypotheses_not_documented.statistical_test_needed: Regress RY.TO weekly returns on Brent with a market control; event-study around large oil moves; compare with sector PCL history across a full oil cycle (2015-16, 2020).
